newsitem.title: UK: U.S. Treasuries seen underperforming Europe debt.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasuries seen underperforming Europe debt.

text.p: Bullish or bearish, U.S. Treasuries are likely to underperform European debt in the weeks ahead, analysts said on Wednesday.

In the short term the doom and gloom tone for global bonds has lessened but even a sturdier U.S. market has left the yield spread above European levels at historically wide levels. And analysts say it could go wider.
"The fact the U.S. economy is growing well above trend, particularly with consumer spending strong, that is a cause for concern," said Ian Amstad, senior economist at Bankers Trust in London.
Amstad said recent U.S. inflation numbers were reassuring but they represented a lagging indicator and the market was more focused on growth-oriented data.
He said Europe on the other hand was starting to see growth but it was lopsided and dependent on exports.
The spread between 10-year U.S. and German government debt showing a yield premium in the U.S. of around 118 basis points (1.18 percentage point) is at its widest level for years.
"Historically it's very wide but our guess is that it will probably grind higher," said Amstad.
Kim Thomsen, head of fixed income at Danske Invest in Copenhagen, concurred, saying: "The market is very vulnerable to further indications of high growth."
Danske Invest is Denmark's largest investment fund, with $2 billion invested overall and $250 million in fixed income.
"What we have seen is a normal correction in an oversold market," he said, referring to the generally stronger tone in bond markets worldwide.
But even in that environment, the U.S. market has failed to narrow the yield gap.
Thomsen said the Treasury/German Bund spread could widen to the 125 to 140 basis point area, although he said that might be its peak.

Brian Venables, senior bond analyst at ABN AMRO Hoare Govett in Amsterdam, said that in broad terms European bond markets were in a better fundamental position because of the contrasts in economic growth.
"The U.S. has it, Germany doesn't," he said.

Amstad of Bankers Trust said that even though European growth will start to come through this year, there was a fiscal drag on Germany because of the process of European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).
Many economists also expect the bears to reassert themselves in the bond markets.
"The U.S. got a slight reprieve from the inflation data yesterday," Venables said. "But one set of inflation data does not change the story that the Fed is in a tightening cycle."
U.S. consumer prices rose only modestly in March, showing a 0.1 percent increase after a 0.3 percent rise in February.
Thomsen said the U.S. long bond yield could move into the 7.25 to 7.50 percent area, while Bund yields were likely to peak up in the 6.00 to 6.25 percent zone.
On a more upbeat note, he said this year was different from 1994, when bond markets suffered a serious bear phase.
Back then, he said, most market players were long of bonds. That made the price falls all the more heavy when the Federal Reserve began a series of interest rate increases.
Investors have gone into 1997 with a more mixed outlook, keeping portfolio durations neutral to short, Thomsen said.
